opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, the biggest adjustment is how much you suddenly have to build yourself. At Google, so much is just there. You have enormous compute, mature infrastructure, internal tools that have been refined over years, and teams down the hall who are world experts in almost anything you might need. You can focus almost entirely on the research question in front of you.

When you start a company, all of that disappears. You think about where your compute comes from, how you're paying for it, how you set up training and evaluation pipelines from scratch, and how you hire people when you can't point to a famous brand. Every decision carries more weight because resources are finite and mistakes are expensive.

The other shift is mental. In a big research lab, success can mean a strong paper or an interesting result that moves the field forward. In a startup, the question is always whether this matters to a user or a customer, and whether it matters soon. You have to be much more disciplined about what you work on and what you say no to, even when an idea is scientifically fascinating.

And there's simply more on your plate: fundraising, recruiting, culture, product, on top of the technical work. That context-switching is hard when you've spent years going deep on research problems.

But it's also what makes it exciting. You move faster, you own the whole thing end to end, and you get to shape a team and a culture from day one. The difficulty is a big part of why it feels worth doing.

r001.rationale: The response describes Google’s mature infrastructure and internal tools, but does not attribute a steep technical learning curve to Google generally lacking open-source tool use.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the hardest part wasn't technical. At Google, when you have an idea, the infrastructure is just there. You want to train a model, you file a request and a few thousand TPUs show up. You want data, there's a team that already cleaned it. You want to ship something, there's a launch process, legal, privacy review, all of it running in the background so you never have to think about it. I didn't realize how much of my productivity was actually the organization's productivity until I left and all of it disappeared at once.

So the first few months were humbling. I'd spend a whole day on something like getting cloud credits approved or figuring out why our data pipeline was silently dropping records, and I'd go home thinking, I used to run research teams, and today I debugged a cron job. You have to make peace with that pretty quickly or you'll be miserable.

The second thing, which I underestimated, is the shift from being right to being useful. In research, the reward is for the clever idea, the paper, the result that moves a benchmark. In a company, nobody cares whether the idea is clever. They care whether it solves their problem by Thursday. I've had to kill things I was genuinely proud of because customers didn't want them, and that's a very different emotional muscle than having a paper rejected.

And then there's the people side. At Google I could hire from an enormous internal pool of people who already knew how to work. Now every hire is a bet with real money, and if I pick wrong it costs us months. I spend way more time thinking about who to bring on and how to keep a very small team pointed in the same direction than I ever expected.

But I'd say the flip side is also true. The thing that's hard about leaving, that nothing is handed to you, is exactly what makes it worth doing. When something works now, it's because we made it work. There's no ambiguity about that, and I've found that very motivating.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the hardest part was not technical and attributes the transition’s difficulty to losing Google’s infrastructure, support teams, and processes. It does not mention Google’s lack of open-source tool use.

astra-6.text:
The biggest adjustment is that you’re building the company at the same time you’re building the product. At Google, there’s a lot of infrastructure around you—tools, processes, and people with deep expertise. In a new company, you have to decide which of those things you need now and which can wait.

That makes prioritization really important. You can have lots of interesting technical ideas, but you have to ask: What’s the most important thing we need to learn from a customer? What should we build to learn that? The freedom to move quickly is exciting, but it also means being much more deliberate about where you spend your time.

r001.rationale: The response discusses Google’s infrastructure and prioritization, but does not attribute a steep technical learning curve to Google’s general lack of open-source tool use.

sol-6.1.text:
One of the biggest adjustments is how much context switching you have to do. At Google, you have infrastructure and teams that let you focus deeply on a particular problem. When you’re building a company, you might be working on the technology in the morning, recruiting in the afternoon, and figuring out an operational issue at night. All of those things matter, but they compete for your attention.

The other challenge is deciding what not to do. There are so many interesting technical directions, but you have to connect them to something people actually need. That means getting feedback early and being willing to change your assumptions. You have more freedom, but you also have to create the focus yourself.

r001.rationale: The response describes context switching, recruiting and operations, and prioritizing customer needs. It does not attribute a steep technical learning curve to Google’s lack of open-source tool use.
